newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Wives quit barracks as Zaire city get rebel jitters.
newsitem.headline: Wives quit barracks as Zaire city get rebel jitters.

text.p: Soldiers' families, fearing the arrival of Laurent Kabila's rebel forces, packed up their things and deserted an army barracks on Tuesday as Zaire's second city Lubumbashi got the jitters.
"Kabila's coming so we're going to the township," said one woman who had rolled her foam mattress on her head and bundled up a few belongings.

She was one in a column of scores of wives and children who had left the Kimbembe army base, some 12 km (seven miles) from the town centre, to head for what they hope will be the relative safety of the populous poor part of town.

Panic had earlier swept the central market amid rumours that rebels were now only some 80 to 100 km (50 to 70 miles) north of the city towards the town of Kasenga -- meaning pillage-prone retreating Zairean troops were even nearer.
Eyewitnesses said masses of people fled the colonial-style business district to La Cite, the African centre of town that sits alongside it. Things calmed later and people returned.
Nerves first started to fray 11 days ago when rebels, vowing to topple Zaire's unpopular president, Mobutu Sese Seko, took the third city of Kisangani and said Lubumbashi was next.

Expatriate sources said regular local soldiers and units of the once elite presidential guard had been sent north on the road to Kasenga to stop retreating Zairean troops entering the city itself and looting it as they have done elsewhere.
The sources, with contacts in the countryside, said the army had pulled out of towns along Lake Mwero, further north, and headed to Kasenga, some 220 km (130 miles) from Lubumbashi.
"The rebels are still a fair bit further north by the lake, but we cannot say exactly where," one said.

The city was already tense in the morning after foreign French-language radio stations, eagerly listened to by locals desperate for information about the five-month war, reported rebel claims that they were only about 200 km (120 miles) away.
No major outbreaks of looting have taken place, partly due to stepped-up military patrols and checkpoints at night.
Locals and expatriates are pinning hopes on the fact that Lubumbashi is in a near cul-de-sac jutting into Zambia.
They assume that the soldiers know they would have no safe escape route with their booty if rebels also cut the railway line that links the city to the diamond-rich Kasai province.
